newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Foreign firms show interest in Bulgaria gas storagE.
newsitem.headline: Foreign firms show interest in Bulgaria gas storagE.

text.p: Turkish and French firms have shown interest in the expansion of Bulgaria's natural gas storage capacity and in the construction of a new facility, energy officials said on Tuesday.

They said the Chiren gas storage facility in northern Bulgaria needs to increase capacity to some four billion cubic metres from the current one billion and France's Gaz de France could invest in its construction.
Officials said 57 million levs had already been invested in enlarging the Chiren capacity, currently 2.5 million cubic metres per day.
Turkey, which expects to increase its Russian gas imports via Bulgaria to about 20 billion cubic metres in the next few years, is also interested in the construction of a new gas storage facility.

Bulgaria's state-owned gas monopolist Bulgargas is considering the construction of a new storage facility using abandoned salt caverns in the village of Mirovo near the industrial area of Devnya in northeastern Bulgaria.
Natural gas was found under the caverns.

Bulgargas officials said a Turkish firm had shown interest in investing in the construction of new storage in Mirovo, which would help Turkey when Russian gas supplies fall sharply in cold winters. They did not name the company.
For the last nine years a gas pipeline has linked Bulgaria with Turkey. Bulgaria receives eight percent in transit tax from the annual quantity supplied to Turkey by Russia.
Bulgaria imports 3.34 billion cubic metres of Russian gas per year in return for its participation in construction work at Russia's Yamburg gas field under a 20-year intergovernmental agreement.

The first 10 years of the agreement during which Bulgaria receives natural gas without cash payment, expires in 1997. Bulgargas plans to offer the Russian side a barter deal for the remaining 10 years. Negotiations will be held at the end of the year.
Bulgaria relies on Russian gas supplies to meet 95.5 percent of its demand. It also imports an annual two billion cubic metres of Russian natural gas for cash payment.

Bulgaria has a 2,200-km pipeline network including 625 km of transit pipelines, receiving and transmitting gas from outside the country, which may become a transit gas corridor from Russia to the Balkans and Italy.
Bulgarian-Russian joint gas stock company Topenergy, in which Russia's gas giant Gazprom holds a 50-percent stake, plans to sell and deliver Russian gas to the Balkans via Bulgaria.
Topenergy plans also to build gas storage facilities in Bulgaria over the next 10-15 years with a capacity of 3.5-4 billion cubic metres in order to ensure constant supplies to the Balkan countries.
